1.title: Virtual Networks, Peering, Routes and Public IPs
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: Virtual Networks, Peering, Routes and Public I P s. It covers the exam area Implement and manage virtual networking. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Create and configure virtual networks and subnets. Create and configure virtual network peering. Configure public I P addresses. Configure user-defined network routes. Troubleshoot network connectivity. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Implement and manage virtual networking (fifteen-twenty percent). Exam format: one hundred minutes; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official Microsoft Learn A Z-one hundred four study guide, skills measured as of October twenty-six, two thousand twenty-three.

1.title: Virtual networks and subnets
1.text: Virtual networks and subnets. An Azure virtual network (V net) is your private network in Azure. It has one or more address spaces (C I D R ranges such as ten dot zero dot zero dot zero slash sixteen ) divided into subnets. Scope. A V net lives in one region and one subscription. Subnets. Each subnet is a range inside the address space; resources get private I P s from it. Reserved addresses. Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet (network, gateway, two for D N S, broadcast). Default. Resources in a V net can talk to each other, and outbound internet works by default. Special subnets. Gateway Subnet (V P N or Express Route gateway), Azure Bastion Subnet, Azure Firewall Subnet.

1.title: Virtual networks and subnets, continued
1.text: Virtual networks and subnets. The figure shows this: A virtual network with two subnets and reserved addresses. Exam tip: Address spaces of peered or connected V nets must not overlap. Plan C I D R ranges before you build.

1.title: Virtual network peering
1.text: Virtual network peering. Peering connects two V nets so they communicate over the Microsoft backbone with low latency, as if they were one network. Types. V net peering (same region) and global V net peering (different regions). Direction. Create a peering in both directions (each V net has a link to the other). Overlap. Address spaces must not overlap. Transitive. Not transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C unless peered directly (or traffic is routed through a network virtual appliance or gateway).

1.title: Virtual network peering, continued
1.text: Virtual network peering. Gateway transit. One V net can share its V P N (virtual private network) gateway with a peer (Allow gateway transit and Use remote gateways). Exam tip: Peering is not transitive. "A and C cannot communicate through B" is the typical trap.

1.title: Public IP addresses
1.text: Public I P addresses. skew. Basic (being retired ) and Standard (zone-redundant, secure by default: closed to inbound traffic until an N S G allows it). Assignment. Static (address does not change) or Dynamic (can change when the resource is deallocated; Basic only). Attach to. N I C of a V M, load balancer frontend, nat gateway, Bastion, V P N gateway. Standard public I P s and Standard load balancers must match S K Us.

1.title: Routes
1.text: Routes. Azure has system routes by default (within the V net, to the internet, between peered V nets). Override them with a route table of user-defined routes (U D Rs) associated to subnets. Address prefix. The destination (for example zero dot zero dot zero dot zero slash zero ). Next hop type. Virtual appliance (give its I P), Virtual network gateway, Virtual network, Internet, None (drops traffic). Use. Force traffic through a firewall or network virtual appliance; block a destination with next hop None. Most specific route wins (longest prefix match); a U D R beats a system route with the same prefix.

1.title: Routes, continued
1.text: Routes. The figure shows this: A route table forcing outbound traffic through a firewall appliance.

1.title: Troubleshooting connectivity
1.text: Troubleshooting connectivity. I P flow verify. Is this packet allowed or denied by an N S G rule (and which rule)? Next hop. Where does traffic from this V M go next? Connection troubleshoot. Can A reach B, and where does it fail? Effective security rules or effective routes. The combined rules and routes that apply to a N I C. Topology or packet capture or N S G flow logs. Visualize, capture, log traffic. Exam tip: "Why can't this V M reach that endpoint?" equals check effective routes, effective security rules, I P flow verify and next hop.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. V net A is peered with V net B, and B with V net C. Can a V M in A reach a V M in C? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: No, peering is not transitive. Peering is not transitive; A and C need their own peering or routing.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which requirement must be true to peer two V nets? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Their address spaces must not overlap. Overlapping address spaces cannot be peered.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. All outbound traffic from a subnet must go through a firewall appliance. What should be configured? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: A user-defined route with next hop type Virtual appliance. U D Rs override system routes to force traffic through an appliance.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. How many I P addresses does Azure reserve in each subnet? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: five. Azure reserves five addresses per subnet.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. An administrator wants to know whether a network security group is blocking traffic to a V M. Which Network Watcher tool fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: I P flow verify. I P flow verify shows whether a packet is allowed or denied and by which rule.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A Standard skew public I P is attached to a V M. What is its default inbound behavior? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Closed until an N S G allows traffic. Standard public I P s are secure by default.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the largest unit of a V net's address plan? Answer: The address space (C I D R range). Question two. Is V net peering transitive? Answer: No. Question three. How many peering links does a full peering need? Answer: Two, one in each direction.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is a U D R? Answer: A user-defined route in a route table that overrides system routes. Question five. Which next hop type drops traffic? Answer: None. Question six. Which tool shows the next hop for traffic from a V M? Answer: Network Watcher next hop.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. V net: one region; subnets; five reserved addresses; special subnets. Peering: both directions; no overlap; not transitive; global peering across regions. Public I P: Standard (secure by default, zone-redundant) versus Basic; static or dynamic. Routes: U D R with next hop; longest prefix wins; U D R beats system route. Troubleshoot: I P flow verify, next hop, connection troubleshoot, effective rules and routes.
